a. **Inner lining of the intestine: columnar epithelium** (epithelial tissue). Its tall, pillar-like cells carry **microvilli** on the free surface and are mixed with mucus-secreting **goblet cells**; it helps in secretion and absorption.
b. **Heart wall: cardiac muscle** (muscular tissue). Cardiac muscles form the **myocardium** of the heart wall; they are striated, involuntary muscles joined by intercalated discs.
c. **Skin: stratified epithelium** (compound epithelial tissue) forms the epidermis of the skin, where it gives protection. The dermis below it is **dense irregular connective tissue**.
d. **Nerve cord: nervous tissue**, made up of **neurons** (nerve cells) and supporting **neuroglial cells**.
e. **Inner lining of the buccal cavity: ciliated epithelium** (epithelial tissue), as in the buccal cavity of the frog. Its cilia move materials in contact with them in a specific direction.
[Note: the chapter names ciliated epithelium only for the buccal cavity of the frog; it does not state the type of epithelium lining the human buccal cavity.]

The layer of fat below the skin is **adipose tissue**, made of adipocytes that store fat as droplets. Adipose tissue is a **good insulator**, so this layer reduces the loss of body heat in a cold climate and keeps the animal warm. Because it stores fat, it is also a **good source of energy** that the animal can draw on, and it acts as a **shock absorber**.

The ear pinna is supported by **elastic cartilage**. Its matrix contains **elastic fibres**, which are made of elastin and are elastic in nature, so the pinna can be folded and twisted and then returns to its shape; this cartilage gives support and maintains the shape of the body part. The tip of the nose is supported by **hyaline cartilage**, whose gel-like matrix has only very fine **collagen fibres** and no elastic fibres. Hyaline cartilage is compressible and acts as a shock absorber, but it lacks the elastic fibres needed to be folded and twisted like the pinna.
[Note: the textbook lists the ear lobe and the tip of the nose under elastic cartilage. The cartilage of the pinna is elastic cartilage, but the soft ear lobe itself has no cartilage, and the cartilage of the nose tip is hyaline cartilage.]

The tissue responsible is **nervous tissue**, whose **neurons** generate and conduct impulses and bring about quick communication within the body. The heat stimulus is carried from the skin to the central nervous system by an **afferent (sensory) neuron**. **Interneurons** (association neurons) in the CNS process it and activate the appropriate **efferent (motor) neuron**, which carries the impulse to the effector, the skeletal muscles of the arm. These muscles contract and Sharad pulls his hand away.
[Note: the chapter does not name this quick automatic response (reflex action) or describe its pathway as a reflex arc.]

Long bones contain **spongy bone**, whose reticular matrix is arranged as trabeculae and which contains **red bone marrow**. The injury to Priya's long bone probably damaged this spongy bone and its red bone marrow. Red bone marrow is where blood cells, including red blood cells, are formed, so with less marrow working fewer red blood cells were produced, and this led to **anaemia**.
[Note: the chapter does not state that red bone marrow forms red blood cells, and it does not define anaemia; blood is left to the chapter 'Circulation' in class XII.]

**Smooth (non-striated) muscle**, the **circular muscles** of the iris that surround the pupil. Smooth muscles are involuntary and are innervated by the **autonomic nervous system**, so in bright light they contract on their own and the pupil becomes smaller. They may be arranged around the circumference of an organ as circular muscles, and their contraction narrows the opening.
[Note: the chapter does not describe the iris or name the muscles of the eye; it states only that smooth muscles may be arranged as circular muscles around an organ.]

**Cell junctions** are the **junctional complexes** by which epithelial cells are connected to each other laterally as well as to the basement membrane. There are five types:
1. **Tight junctions (TJs):** maintain cell polarity and prevent lateral diffusion of proteins and ions.
2. **Adherens junctions (AJs):** are involved in various signalling pathways and transcriptional regulation.
3. **Gap junctions (GJs):** intercellular connections that allow the passage of ions and small molecules between cells, as well as the exchange of chemical messages between cells.
4. **Desmosomes (Ds):** provide mechanical strength to epithelial tissue, cardiac muscles and meninges.
5. **Hemidesmosomes (HDs):** allow the cells to adhere strongly to the underlying basement membrane, and maintain tissue homeostasis by signalling.

The diagram shows **areolar tissue** (Fig. 10.9), a loose connective tissue. Labels: **macrophage**, **matrix**, **fibroblast**, **collagen fibres (white fibres)**, **yellow fibres**, **mast cell**.

Structure:
1. The **matrix** is semisolid, jelly-like and viscous; it is the ground substance formed of polysaccharides produced by fibroblasts.
2. The matrix contains two types of fibres. **White fibres** are made of **collagen** and give tensile strength to the tissue. **Yellow fibres** are made of **elastin** and are elastic in nature.
3. Four types of cells are present. **Fibroblasts** are large, flat cells with branching processes that produce the fibres and the polysaccharides of the matrix.
4. **Mast cells** are oval cells that secrete **heparin** and **histamine**.
5. **Macrophages** are amoeboid, phagocytic cells.
6. **Fat cells (adipocytes)** have an eccentric nucleus and store fat.

Areolar tissue acts as a packing material, helps in the healing process and connects different organs or layers of tissues. It is found under the skin, between muscles and bones, around organs and blood vessels, and in the peritoneum.
[Note: the textbook says the matrix of loose connective tissue is made up of gelatin; the matrix is a jelly-like ground substance of polysaccharides, as the same page states for the fibroblasts.]

1. In a **multipolar neuron** the **cyton** (cell body) is star shaped and gives out more than two processes: **only one axon**, and all the others are **dendrons**.
2. The cyton contains granular cytoplasm called **neuroplasm** and a centrally placed **nucleus** with a nucleolus. The neuroplasm contains mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, RER and **Nissl's granules**, which are made of RNA.
3. **Dendrons** are short, branched processes. Their fine branches are called **dendrites**, and they carry impulses towards the cyton.
4. The **axon** is a single, elongated, cylindrical process that starts from a funnel-shaped area of the cyton called the **axon hillock**.
5. The axon is bounded by the **axolemma**, and its protoplasm, the **axoplasm**, contains many mitochondria and neurofibrils.
6. The axon is enclosed in a fatty **myelin sheath**, whose outer covering is the **neurilemma**. Both are parts of the **Schwann cell**, whose nucleus lies at the periphery.
7. The myelin sheath is absent at intervals along the axon; these places are the **nodes of Ranvier**.
8. The axon ends in a terminal arborization called the **telodendron**.

| Point | Smooth muscles | Skeletal muscles |
|---|---|---|
| Location | In the walls of visceral organs and blood vessels, hence called visceral muscles | Attached to bones |
| Shape of fibre and nuclei | Spindle-shaped (fusiform), unbranched fibre with a single nucleus at the centre | Long syncytial fibre with several nuclei, shifted to the periphery |
| Striations | Absent, so they are non-striated | Present, because dark (A) and light (I) bands of neighbouring myofibrils correspond |
| Contraction and control | Slow, sustained, involuntary contractions; innervated by the autonomic nervous system | Quick, strong, voluntary contractions; bring about voluntary movements of the body |
| Contractile proteins | Less myosin and more actin | More myosin and less actin than smooth muscles |

|  | Cell / Tissue / Muscles | Functions |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | Cardiac muscles | Form the myocardium of the heart wall and contract as a unit; intercalated discs help in quick transfer of the stimulus |
| 2. | **Tendons** | Connect skeletal muscles to bones. |
| 3. | Chondroblast cells | Immature cartilage-forming cells; they mature into chondrocytes |
| 4. | **Mast cells** | Secrete heparin and histamine |

In mammals some cardiac muscles can generate impulses on their own, which makes the heart myogenic. Tendons are dense regular connective tissue with bundles of white fibres that give them tensile strength. Chondroblasts lie just below the perichondrium. Mast cells are oval cells of areolar tissue.

| 'A' Group | 'B' Group |
|---|---|
| 1. Muscle | b. Sarcolemma |
| 2. Bone | c. Periosteum |
| 3. Nerve cell | d. Neurilemma |
| 4. Cartilage | a. Perichondrium |

1. The **sarcolemma** is the membrane that covers each muscle fibre.
2. The **periosteum** is the outer tough membrane that encloses the matrix of bone.
3. The **neurilemma** is the outer covering of the myelin sheath around the axon of a nerve cell.
4. The **perichondrium** is the sheath of collagenous fibres that delimits the matrix of cartilage.
